stem: What is the fundamental architectural difference between a Docker container and a virtual machine?

options.text: A container runs its own guest kernel on a lightweight hypervisor
options.why: That describes a VM or a micro-VM such as Firecracker, not a standard container.

options.text: Containers share the host kernel; each VM boots its own guest kernel
options.why: A container is an isolated host process, while a VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS.

options.text: Containers emulate the CPU, so any architecture runs unchanged on any host
options.why: Containers execute native instructions; running another CPU architecture needs QEMU emulation.

options.text: A VM shares the host kernel, but a container brings its own minimal kernel
options.why: This reverses the model: the image ships userspace files only, never a kernel.

explanation: A virtual machine virtualises hardware, so each VM boots its own kernel on top of a hypervisor. A container is one or more ordinary processes on the host kernel, given an isolated view of the system with namespaces and resource limits with cgroups. That is why containers start in milliseconds and pack densely, and also why their isolation boundary (the shared kernel) is weaker than a VM's.
reference: Docker docs: What is a container?

stem: A process running inside a Docker container on a Linux host is an ordinary host process: with enough privileges you can see it in `ps` output on the host.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the container's processes run on the host kernel and appear in the host's process table, just with a different PID.

options.text: False
options.why: They are not hidden in a VM; namespaces only change what the container sees, not what the host sees.

explanation: Namespaces isolate the container's view of the system, but the host sees everything. `ps aux` on a Linux host lists container processes alongside other processes, under host PIDs that differ from the PIDs seen inside the container. (On Docker Desktop for Mac or Windows the processes live inside the Linux VM, not on the macOS or Windows host.)

stem: Which Linux kernel feature does Docker use to cap how much memory a container may use?

options.text: Mount namespaces
options.why: Namespaces change what a process can see, not how much it can use.

options.text: The overlay2 storage driver
options.why: overlay2 builds the layered root filesystem; it sets no memory limits.

options.text: Control groups (cgroups)
options.why: cgroups account for and limit resources such as memory, CPU and the number of processes.

options.text: The seccomp filter profile
options.why: seccomp restricts which system calls a process may make, not its memory.

explanation: Namespaces provide isolation (what a process can see), and cgroups provide resource control (how much it can use). `docker run --memory=512m` writes the limit into the container's cgroup, and the kernel enforces it.

stem: Match each Linux namespace with what it isolates for a container.

options.text: Process IDs, so the container's first process can be PID 1
Network interfaces, routing tables and ports
The set of mounted filesystems the process sees
The hostname and NIS domain name

explanation: Each namespace type wraps one global resource. PID gives the container its own process numbering, NET its own interfaces, routes and port space, MNT its own mount table (and so its own root filesystem), and UTS its own hostname. Docker creates all of them, plus IPC and usually a cgroup namespace, for every container.

stem: On a current Docker Engine for Linux, what is the name of the default storage driver that assembles the container's layered root filesystem? Type the driver name.
explanation: overlay2 is the default and recommended storage driver on all actively supported Linux distributions. It uses the kernel's OverlayFS to stack the read-only image layers under a thin writable container layer. (Newer Docker versions can also use the containerd image store with snapshotters, which use overlayfs underneath.)

stem: Why does a container typically start in well under a second while a virtual machine takes much longer?

options.text: Containers resume a cached, hibernated kernel image
options.why: There is no per-container kernel to resume; the host kernel is already running.

options.text: Docker pre-boots a pool of idle VMs and hands one to each container
options.why: Docker Engine on Linux runs no VMs at all for containers.

options.text: Starting one just launches a process with namespaces and cgroups
options.why: The kernel is already up, so only the application process has to start.

options.text: Containers skip the dynamic linker because images are statically linked
options.why: Most images use dynamically linked programs; linking is not what makes startup fast.

explanation: A VM must boot firmware, a kernel and an init system. A container reuses the host kernel that is already running: the runtime creates namespaces, configures cgroups, mounts the image layers and executes one process. That is close to the cost of starting a normal process.
reference: Docker docs: What is a container?

stem: Which two are real advantages of containers over full virtual machines? (Choose two.)

options.text: The same image runs with the same userspace on a laptop, CI and production
options.why: The image packages the application with its libraries, removing "works on my machine" drift.

options.text: Many more workloads fit on one host, because there is no guest OS per instance
options.why: Without a kernel and OS per instance, memory and CPU overhead is far lower.

options.text: Stronger isolation, because each container has its own private kernel
options.why: Containers share the host kernel; VMs give the stronger isolation boundary.

options.text: Any OS kernel can be run, such as a Windows kernel on a Linux host
options.why: A container uses the host kernel, so it can only run software for that kernel.

options.text: Data written inside a container survives removal unless you opt out
options.why: The writable layer is deleted with the container; persistence needs volumes or bind mounts.

explanation: Containers give reproducible environments (the image carries the userspace) and high density (no guest OS per instance). They do not give stronger isolation than VMs, cannot change the kernel, and their writable layer is ephemeral.

stem: A developer runs Linux containers with Docker Desktop on macOS. Where do those containers actually run?

options.text: Directly on the macOS (Darwin) kernel through a syscall shim
options.why: Darwin cannot run Linux binaries natively, and Docker ships no such shim.

options.text: Inside a small Linux VM managed by Docker Desktop
options.why: Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM, and the Docker Engine and containers live inside it.

options.text: In Rosetta 2, translating Linux syscalls
options.why: Rosetta translates CPU instructions for macOS apps, not Linux system calls.

options.text: On a remote Docker Cloud host that Desktop signs in to by default
options.why: Docker Desktop runs everything locally unless you configure a remote context.

explanation: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. On macOS (and on Windows with the WSL 2 or Hyper-V backend) Docker Desktop starts a small Linux VM, runs the Docker Engine inside it, and forwards the CLI, ports and file sharing between the host and the VM.

stem: Inside a container, `ps` shows the application as PID 1. On the Linux host, an administrator runs `ps aux | grep myapp`. What do they see?

options.text: Nothing, because container processes are hidden from the host
options.why: PID namespaces hide host processes from the container, not the reverse.

options.text: The same process listed as PID 1, which replaces the host init
options.why: The host's PID 1 is still its own init; the container's PID 1 is a different number on the host.

options.text: The same process under an ordinary, different host PID such as 48213
options.why: A PID namespace gives the process a second PID inside the container; the host sees its real PID.

options.text: A qemu process that wraps the container's entire process tree
options.why: No emulator is involved for native Linux containers; the app runs directly on the kernel.

explanation: PID namespaces are nested: a process has one PID in each namespace it belongs to. Inside the container the first process is PID 1; in the host's (parent) namespace it has a normal PID. That is why you can `kill` or `strace` a container process from the host using its host PID.

stem: A container writes `/tmp/report.csv` into its own filesystem, with no volume or bind mount. The container is then stopped and removed with `docker rm`. What happens to the file?

options.text: It is merged into the image, so new containers from the image see it
options.why: Images are read-only; only `docker commit` or a build creates new image layers.

options.text: Docker moves it into an anonymous volume that `docker volume ls` lists
options.why: Anonymous volumes exist only for paths declared as volumes, which `/tmp` is not here.

options.text: It is deleted along with the container's writable layer
options.why: The writable layer belongs to the container and is removed by `docker rm`.

options.text: It stays until `docker system prune` runs
options.why: Removal deletes the layer immediately; prune is for unused images, networks and volumes.

explanation: Every container gets a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image layers. It survives `docker stop` and restarts, but `docker rm` deletes it. Anything that must outlive the container belongs in a volume or bind mount.
reference: Docker docs: Storage drivers (container and layers)

stem: Order the components a `docker run` request passes through on a Linux host, from the command you type to the process that creates the container.

options.text: The `docker` CLI client
The Docker daemon, `dockerd`, via the Engine API
containerd, which manages the container lifecycle
The containerd shim (`containerd-shim-runc-v2`)
runc, which creates the namespaces and cgroups and starts the process

explanation: The CLI calls the Engine REST API on `dockerd`. dockerd asks containerd to create and start the container. containerd starts a shim for that container, and the shim invokes runc, the OCI runtime, which sets up namespaces and cgroups, starts the process and then exits. The shim stays as the parent of the container process.
reference: Docker docs: Docker architecture; containerd docs

stem: What is runc's role in the Docker stack?

options.text: It is the registry client that pulls and unpacks image layers
options.why: Pulling and unpacking images is done by dockerd and containerd, not runc.

options.text: It is the low-level OCI runtime that starts the container
options.why: runc reads an OCI bundle (config.json plus a rootfs) and spawns the isolated process.

options.text: It is the long-running daemon that serves the Docker Engine API
options.why: That daemon is dockerd; runc is a short-lived command-line tool.

options.text: It is the plugin that wires up docker0
options.why: Networking is configured by dockerd's libnetwork, not by runc.

explanation: runc is the reference implementation of the OCI runtime specification. Given a bundle (a `config.json` and a root filesystem), it creates namespaces and cgroups, applies security settings and starts the process. It exits once the container is running, and the containerd shim stays behind as the parent.

stem: The Open Container Initiative (OCI) publishes specifications that let different tools interoperate. Which three does it define? (Choose three.)

options.text: A runtime specification for how to run a container from a bundle
options.why: The runtime-spec defines config.json and the container lifecycle that runc implements.

options.text: An image specification for manifests, configs and filesystem layers
options.why: The image-spec lets an image built by one tool run under another.

options.text: A distribution specification for the registry push and pull API
options.why: The distribution-spec standardises how registries store and serve content.

options.text: The Compose file format for multi-container applications
options.why: The Compose Specification is a separate project, not an OCI spec.

options.text: The Dockerfile syntax and its build instructions
options.why: Dockerfile syntax is defined by Docker and BuildKit, not by the OCI.

options.text: A scheduling API for running containers across a cluster
options.why: Cluster orchestration (such as Kubernetes) is outside the OCI's scope.

explanation: The OCI maintains three specifications: runtime-spec, image-spec and distribution-spec. Together they let you build an image with one tool (Docker, Buildah), push it to any compliant registry, and run it with any compliant runtime (runc, crun, gVisor).

stem: On a cgroup v2 host, `docker run --memory=512m` writes the container's hard memory limit into which cgroup interface file?

options.text: `memory.limit_in_bytes`
options.why: That is the cgroup v1 file; cgroup v2 renamed and restructured the interface.

options.text: `memory.high`
options.why: memory.high is a throttling threshold that triggers reclaim, not the hard cap.

options.text: `memory.max`
options.why: memory.max is the cgroup v2 hard limit; exceeding it triggers the OOM killer.

options.text: `memory.swap.max`
options.why: That file limits swap usage, which is separate from the memory limit.

explanation: cgroup v2 uses a single unified hierarchy with new file names. `memory.max` is the hard limit (the old `memory.limit_in_bytes`), `memory.high` is a softer throttle point, and `memory.swap.max` caps swap. Docker writes `--memory` into `memory.max`.

stem: Ten containers started from the same 300 MB image each store their own full 300 MB copy of the image filesystem on disk.

options.text: True
options.why: The image layers are read-only and shared; each container only adds its own thin writable layer.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the read-only image layers are shared, and each container only gets a thin writable layer for its own changes.

explanation: Union filesystems let every container use the same read-only image layers. Each container adds only a writable layer for files it creates or changes, so ten containers from one image cost roughly one copy of the image plus their individual changes. `docker ps --size` shows each container's writable-layer size separately from the shared "virtual" size.
reference: Docker docs: Storage drivers (container size on disk)

stem: Match each tool with the description that fits it best.

options.text: A daemonless container engine with a Docker-compatible CLI
A runtime daemon that manages images and container lifecycles for Docker and Kubernetes
A low-level OCI runtime that creates the container process
A lightweight runtime built only for the Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface

explanation: Podman runs containers without a central daemon. containerd is the lifecycle and image daemon underneath both Docker and many Kubernetes nodes. runc is the OCI runtime they all use to actually create the process. CRI-O is a minimal runtime built just to serve the kubelet's Container Runtime Interface.

stem: On a cgroup v2 host, which interface file inside a container's cgroup directory lists the PIDs of the processes that belong to it? Type the file name.
explanation: `cgroup.procs` lists the PIDs in a cgroup, one per line, and writing a PID into it moves that process into the cgroup. That is how a runtime places the container's process under its limits.
reference: kernel.org: Control Group v2 (core interface files)

stem: Two processes run in different containers on the same host with default settings. One cannot attach to the other's System V shared-memory segment. Which namespace prevents this?

options.text: The UTS namespace
options.why: UTS isolates only the hostname and domain name.

options.text: The IPC namespace
options.why: IPC namespaces isolate System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues.

options.text: The user namespace
options.why: User namespaces remap UIDs and GIDs; Docker does not enable them by default.

options.text: The cgroup namespace
options.why: The cgroup namespace only changes how the cgroup hierarchy appears.

explanation: Each Docker container gets its own IPC namespace, so System V shared memory, semaphores and message queues are private to it. Sharing has to be explicit, for example with `--ipc=container:<name>` or `--ipc=shareable`.

stem: A container reads `/etc/app.conf`. Order the places OverlayFS looks for the file, from the first place checked to the last.

options.text: The container's writable upper layer
The topmost (most recent) image layer
The middle image layers, top to bottom
The base image layer

explanation: OverlayFS merges an upper directory over the lower directories. A lookup checks the upper (container) layer first, then each lower layer from the newest down to the base, and the first match wins. That is why a file changed in the container, or in a later image layer, hides older copies below it.
reference: Docker docs: OverlayFS storage driver (how it works)

stem: A container runs with `--memory=512m` on a host with swap disabled. Its process steadily allocates and touches 600 MB of anonymous memory. What happens?

options.text: The kernel lets it exceed the limit, because limits apply only to new processes
options.why: The cgroup limit applies to all processes in the cgroup, including existing ones.

options.text: It is OOM-killed: `OOMKilled: true`, exit code 137
options.why: Anonymous memory can't be reclaimed without swap, so the kernel must kill a process.

options.text: Docker pauses the container until memory frees up, then resumes it
options.why: Docker does not pause containers on memory pressure; the kernel acts directly.

options.text: malloc returns NULL and the app copes
options.why: Linux overcommits, so allocation succeeds and the kill happens when pages are touched.

explanation: When a cgroup reaches `memory.max`, the kernel first tries to reclaim memory, such as page cache. Anonymous memory can't be dropped with no swap, so the OOM killer kills a process inside that cgroup. If it is the main process the container exits with 137 (128 + 9, SIGKILL) and Docker records `OOMKilled: true`. With swap enabled and `--memory-swap` unset, the same container could also use up to 512 MB of swap first.

stem: On a cgroup v2 host, a container is started with `--cpus=1.5`. What does its `cpu.max` file contain?

options.why: Docker uses a 100,000 µs period, so the quota is expressed on that scale.
That is a quota of 150,000 µs per 100,000 µs period: 1.5 CPUs' worth of time.
The first field is the quota and the second the period; this swaps them.
cpu.max takes integer microseconds, never a fractional CPU count.

explanation: `--cpus=1.5` is shorthand for `--cpu-period=100000 --cpu-quota=150000`. In cgroup v2 both go into `cpu.max` as "$QUOTA $PERIOD". In each 100 ms period the container's threads may use 150 ms of CPU time in total, spread across any cores.

stem: On an idle 8-core host, container A is started with `--cpu-shares=512` and container B with `--cpu-shares=1024`. Only A has work to do: it runs 8 busy threads. How much CPU can A use?

options.text: At most one third of the host, because its share is 512 out of 1536
options.why: Shares only apply when containers compete; B is idle here.

options.text: At most half of one core, because 512 is half of the 1024 default
options.why: Shares are relative weights, not a fixed fraction of a core.

options.text: All 8 cores, because shares only matter when CPU is contended
options.why: With no competition, a weighted cgroup can use all spare CPU.

options.text: Nothing until B has used its larger allocation first
options.why: The scheduler never holds an idle CPU back for a cgroup that isn't using it.

explanation: `--cpu-shares` (converted to `cpu.weight` on cgroup v2) is a relative weight that matters only under contention. If both containers were busy, A would get about one third of the CPU and B two thirds. With B idle, A can use every core. For a hard ceiling, use `--cpus` (a quota) or `--cpuset-cpus` (pinning).

stem: With default settings, which two things does a container share with its host instead of getting an isolated copy? (Choose two.)

options.text: The running kernel, so `uname -r` shows the host's kernel version
options.why: There is only one kernel; the image contributes userspace files only.

options.text: The system clock, because Docker does not create a time namespace
options.why: Changing the clock (with CAP_SYS_TIME) would change it for the whole host.

options.text: The hostname, unless `--hostname` is passed
options.why: The UTS namespace gives each container its own hostname, the container ID by default.

options.text: The list of running processes
options.why: The PID namespace hides host processes unless `--pid=host` is used.

options.text: The network interfaces and the ports they listen on
options.why: Each container gets its own network namespace unless `--network host` is used.

explanation: Docker namespaces processes, networking, mounts, the hostname and IPC, but the kernel itself is shared, so `uname -r` shows the host kernel. It also creates no time namespace, so all containers see the host clock.

stem: The Docker daemon is configured with `userns-remap: "default"`, and `/etc/subuid` contains `dockremap:100000:65536`. A container running as root writes a file into a bind-mounted host directory. Who owns the file on the host?

options.text: root (UID 0), because the process is root inside the container
options.why: User namespace remapping exists precisely so that container root isn't host root.

options.text: nobody (UID 65534), because remapped files are always anonymised
options.why: The overflow UID is used for host IDs that can't be mapped, not for writes.

options.text: UID 100000, the start of the dockremap subordinate range
options.why: Container UID 0 maps to host UID 100000, so files are created with that owner.

options.text: The UID of whoever ran `docker run`, taken from the client session
options.why: Docker CLI users never become file owners; the daemon's mapping decides.

explanation: With userns-remap, the daemon puts containers into a user namespace that maps container UID 0 to the first subordinate UID of `dockremap` (100000 here), container UID 1 to 100001, and so on. Files a container writes through a bind mount get those host UIDs. This limits damage after a breakout, but host directories must be owned by the remapped IDs.
reference: Docker docs: Isolate containers with a user namespace

stem: A process in a container deletes `/usr/share/doc/README`, which exists in a read-only image layer. How does overlay2 record the deletion in the container's writable upper directory?

options.text: It deletes the file from the lower image layer in place
options.why: Lower layers are read-only and shared, so they are never modified.

options.text: It writes an empty file with the same name in the upper directory
options.why: An empty file would still appear as a file; the path must vanish.

options.text: It creates a whiteout: a character device with device number 0/0
options.why: OverlayFS treats a 0/0 char device in the upper dir as "this path is deleted".

options.text: It adds the path to a deletion list in the container's config.json
options.why: Deletions live in the filesystem layers, not in the OCI runtime config.

explanation: Lower layers can't change, so OverlayFS marks deletions in the upper directory with whiteouts. A deleted file becomes a character device with device number 0/0, and a deleted directory that is recreated is marked "opaque". The original bytes stay in the image layer, which is also why deleting files in a later build step doesn't shrink an image.

stem: On Docker Desktop for Mac, `npm install` in a container is several times slower when `/app` is a bind mount of the macOS project folder than when `node_modules` is in a named volume. Why?

options.text: Bind mounts disable the overlay2 page cache inside every container
options.why: Bind mounts don't use overlay2 at all; the slowdown comes from file sharing.

options.text: Bind mounts cross the VM boundary; volumes live on the VM's disk
options.why: Each file operation on a bind mount is relayed between macOS and the Linux VM.

options.text: macOS encrypts every file that a Linux container writes to a bind mount
options.why: Docker adds no encryption layer to bind-mounted writes.

options.text: Named volumes are held in RAM, while bind mounts must write to the SSD
options.why: Named volumes live on the VM's virtual disk, not in memory.

explanation: Docker Desktop runs containers in a Linux VM. A bind mount of a macOS folder is served into that VM through a file-sharing layer (virtiofs on recent versions), so metadata-heavy workloads with thousands of small files pay a cross-VM cost per operation. A named volume lives on the VM's own disk and runs at native Linux speed. That's why a common pattern keeps the source bind-mounted and `node_modules` in a volume.
reference: Docker docs: Docker Desktop file sharing; Volumes

stem: An image built only for `linux/arm64` is run on an `amd64` Linux server that has no emulation configured. What happens?

options.text: It runs normally, because containers are portable across any architecture
options.why: Images contain native machine code, so portability stops at the CPU architecture.

options.text: Docker transparently rebuilds the image for amd64 before starting it
options.why: Docker never rebuilds images on `run`; it only pulls a matching variant if one exists.

options.text: It fails with an error such as `exec format error`
options.why: The kernel can't execute ARM binaries on x86 without QEMU registered through binfmt_misc.

options.text: It runs in a Docker compatibility mode
options.why: Docker Desktop includes QEMU emulation, but this is a plain server with none configured.

explanation: Containers share the host kernel and run native code, so the image's architecture must match the CPU unless an emulator is set up. Docker prints a platform-mismatch warning, and the process fails with `exec format error`. Fixes are multi-platform images (an image index with amd64 and arm64 variants) or registering QEMU through binfmt_misc, which is slow.

stem: Windows containers share the Windows host kernel. Under process isolation, the container's base image must be compatible with the host's Windows version, while Hyper-V isolation relaxes this requirement.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: process isolation shares the host kernel, so versions must be compatible; Hyper-V isolation gives each container its own kernel in a utility VM.

options.text: False
options.why: This is accurate: process-isolated Windows containers use the host kernel, and Hyper-V isolation is the way to run other versions.

explanation: Containers share their host kernel on Windows too. A process-isolated Windows container must use a base image whose Windows version is compatible with the host's. Hyper-V isolation runs each container inside a lightweight utility VM with its own kernel, which allows more version combinations at the cost of more overhead.
reference: Microsoft Learn: Windows container version compatibility

stem: Each running container has a containerd shim process as its parent. Which two statements about the shim are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It lets runc exit after starting the container, so no runtime binary stays resident
options.why: runc is short-lived; the shim stays to parent the process.

options.text: It holds the container's stdio and exit status, so containerd and dockerd can restart without killing it
options.why: This decoupling is what makes daemon upgrades and Docker's live-restore possible.

options.text: It is the process that runs as PID 1 inside the container
options.why: PID 1 inside the container is your entrypoint; the shim is outside the namespace.

options.text: It enforces the memory and CPU limits by sampling usage
options.why: The kernel enforces cgroup limits; no userspace process polices them.

options.text: It pulls and verifies image layers before each container start
options.why: Pulling and unpacking images is handled by containerd and dockerd.

explanation: containerd starts one shim per container. The shim calls runc to create the container, then becomes the parent of the container process while runc exits. Because the shim, not containerd or dockerd, owns the process, its stdio and its exit code, those daemons can restart or upgrade without taking running containers down.

stem: Match each `docker run` flag with the cgroup v2 interface file it controls.

options.text: `memory.max`
`cpu.max`
`pids.max`
`cpu.weight`

explanation: `--memory` becomes the hard limit in `memory.max`. `--cpus` becomes a quota and period in `cpu.max`. `--pids-limit` caps the process and thread count in `pids.max`. `--cpu-shares` is converted to a relative `cpu.weight`. Reading these files inside or outside the container shows the limits the kernel actually enforces.
reference: kernel.org: Control Group v2; Docker docs: docker run

stem: You switch a service to rootless Docker. `docker run -p 80:8080 web` now fails, but `-p 8080:8080` works. What explains this, and what is the documented fix?

options.text: Rootless mode blocks all port publishing; you must use host networking instead
options.why: Port publishing works in rootless mode; only privileged ports are restricted.

options.text: Ports below 1024 are privileged; lower `ip_unprivileged_port_start`
options.why: The daemon runs as a normal user, so the usual low-port rule applies.

options.text: Port 80 is reserved by the Docker Desktop VM in rootless setups
options.why: This is a Linux rootless daemon; no Desktop VM is involved.

options.text: The image's USER instruction must be root to publish ports in rootless mode
options.why: The container user doesn't matter; the host-side bind is done by the rootless daemon.

explanation: In rootless mode the daemon and its port forwarder run as an ordinary user, so host ports below 1024 can't be bound by default. Docker's docs suggest lowering `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` (for example to 80), granting `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to rootlesskit, or putting a proxy on the privileged port.

stem: A container's processes keep allocating memory past its `--memory` limit on a host without swap. Put the kernel's response in order.

options.text: The cgroup's usage reaches `memory.max` on a new allocation
The kernel tries to reclaim memory charged to that cgroup, such as page cache
Reclaim can't free enough, so the OOM killer picks a victim inside the cgroup
The main process is killed by SIGKILL and Docker records OOMKilled with exit code 137

explanation: The limit is enforced when an allocation would push usage past `memory.max`. The kernel first reclaims reclaimable memory charged to the cgroup, such as clean page cache. Only if that fails does the cgroup-scoped OOM killer choose a process within that cgroup, so other containers and the host are unaffected. If the victim is the container's main process, the container exits with 137 and `docker inspect` shows `OOMKilled: true`.
reference: kernel.org: Control Group v2 (memory); Docker docs: Resource constraints

stem: A fork bomb runs inside a container started with `--pids-limit=200`, and new `fork()` calls start failing with EAGAIN while the host stays healthy. Which cgroup v2 interface file holds the limit that stopped it? Type the file name.
explanation: `--pids-limit` writes into the pids controller's `pids.max`. Once the cgroup has that many processes and threads, further `fork()` or `clone()` calls fail with EAGAIN, so a runaway container can't exhaust the host's PID space.

stem: A container's entrypoint script starts a log shipper in the background with `shipper &`, then runs `exec server` as PID 1. Later the server crashes and exits. What happens to the log shipper?

options.text: It is re-parented to the host's init and keeps running
options.why: Re-parenting to the host init doesn't happen for processes in a dying PID namespace.

options.text: It becomes the new PID 1 and keeps the container running
options.why: PID 1 is never reassigned; the namespace is torn down when PID 1 exits.

options.text: The kernel kills it with SIGKILL as the PID namespace is torn down
options.why: When a PID namespace's init exits, every other process in it is sent SIGKILL.

options.text: It keeps running, but detached in the background, until `docker rm`
options.why: The process can't outlive its namespace's init.

explanation: A PID namespace's first process acts as its init. When it terminates, the kernel sends SIGKILL to every remaining process in that namespace. So the container stops as soon as its main process exits, and helpers get no chance to flush logs. Run such helpers under a proper init or supervisor, or as a separate container.

stem: A container is started with `--memory=300m` and no `--memory-swap`, on a host that has swap enabled. What is the most memory plus swap it can use before the OOM killer acts?

options.text: 300 MB, because unset `--memory-swap` means no swap at all
options.why: That needs `--memory-swap` set equal to `--memory`.

options.text: 600 MB: 300 MB of memory plus up to 300 MB of swap
options.why: With `--memory-swap` unset, the container may use as much swap as its memory limit.

options.text: Unlimited swap on top of 300 MB, as long as the host has swap
options.why: Unlimited swap requires `--memory-swap=-1`.

options.text: 300 MB plus the host's swappiness percentage of that amount
options.why: Swappiness tunes reclaim preference; it doesn't set an allowance.

explanation: Docker documents that when `--memory` is set and `--memory-swap` is not, the container can use swap up to the same amount as its memory limit, if the host has swap configured. Set `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` to forbid swap, or to -1 for unlimited swap. Without swap on the host, only the 300 MB applies.

stem: A latency-sensitive service runs with `--cpus=1` on a 16-core host. It has 8 worker threads that all become busy when a burst arrives. p99 latency spikes by roughly 90 ms even though average CPU use looks low. What is happening?

options.text: The cgroup pins all 8 threads to a single core, so they queue on it
options.why: `--cpus` sets a time quota, not CPU pinning; threads still run on many cores.

options.text: The quota is used up in ~12.5 ms, then the cgroup is throttled
options.why: Eight threads burn 1 CPU-second of quota per second 8× faster, then wait.

options.text: cpu.weight drops while the container bursts
options.why: Weights are fixed relative shares; nothing lowers them during bursts.

options.text: The kernel migrates the threads between NUMA nodes on every period
options.why: NUMA migration isn't triggered by a quota and wouldn't add a fixed ~90 ms.

explanation: A CFS quota is CPU time per period across all threads: `--cpus=1` gives 100 ms per 100 ms. Eight busy threads on eight cores consume that in about 12.5 ms of wall time, then the cgroup is throttled for the remaining ~87.5 ms. That is a latency stall even though average usage looks fine. `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec` in `cpu.stat` reveal it. Fix it by sizing the quota for bursts, matching worker count to the quota, or using cpusets.
reference: kernel.org: CFS Bandwidth Control; Control Group v2 (cpu)

stem: A container runs with `--cpus=2 --memory=1g` on a host with 16 cores and 64 GiB of RAM, with no LXCFS. Which two commands inside the container report host-wide values rather than the container's limits? (Choose two.)

options.text: `nproc`
options.why: It counts CPUs in the affinity mask, and `--cpus` sets a quota, not affinity, so it prints 16.

options.text: `free -m`
options.why: It reads `/proc/meminfo`, which isn't namespaced, so it shows about 64 GiB.

options.text: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max`
options.why: This reads the container's own cgroup and prints the 1 GiB limit in bytes.

options.text: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max`
options.why: This prints the quota and period, 200000 100000, which reflect the limit.

options.text: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current`
options.why: This shows the container cgroup's own current usage, not a host-wide figure.

explanation: `nproc` uses `sched_getaffinity`, and `--cpus` doesn't change affinity (only `--cpuset-cpus` does), so it reports 16. `free` reads `/proc/meminfo`, which shows host totals. The cgroup files show the real limits. Runtimes that size thread pools or heaps from these host-wide values over-subscribe the container unless they read cgroup limits, as modern JVMs and Go's GOMAXPROCS tools do.
reference: kernel.org: Control Group v2; man7.org: nproc(1), proc(5)

stem: An app in a container calls `rename()` to move a directory that came from an image layer to a new name. On overlay2 the call fails with `EXDEV`, though it works on the host's ext4. What is the documented expectation?

options.text: It is a kernel bug; upgrading the host kernel makes rename atomic again
options.why: This is a documented OverlayFS limitation, not a regression to wait out.

options.text: OverlayFS lacks full rename(2) support; fall back to copy and unlink
options.why: Renaming a lower-layer directory can't be done atomically, so EXDEV is returned.

options.text: The container lacks CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, so the call needs `--privileged`
options.why: Privileges don't change OverlayFS rename semantics.

options.text: Docker remounts image layers read-only each time a rename is attempted
options.why: Lower layers are always read-only; nothing is remounted per call.

explanation: Docker's overlay2 documentation lists rename(2) among OverlayFS's POSIX incompatibilities: renaming a directory that isn't entirely in the upper layer can return EXDEV ("cross-device link"). Applications must detect it and fall back to copy and unlink, as `mv` does. Writing such data to a volume avoids the issue.

stem: On overlay2, a process opens an image file read-only (fd1) and then opens the same path read-write (fd2), triggering a copy-up. It writes through fd2 and reads through fd1. What may it observe on the kernels Docker's docs warn about?

options.text: Both descriptors always see the new bytes, because overlay2 is fully POSIX
options.why: Docker's docs explicitly list this case as a POSIX gap.

options.text: fd1 still reads the old lower-layer file, while fd2 writes to the new upper copy
options.why: fd1 was opened before copy-up, so it can keep pointing at the lower-layer file.

options.text: The second open fails with EBUSY until fd1 is closed
options.why: Opening for write succeeds; the copy-up happens on that open.

options.text: The kernel transparently re-points fd1 at the upper copy on its next read
options.why: No such re-pointing is guaranteed, which is exactly the hazard.

explanation: Copy-up creates a new inode in the upper layer. A descriptor opened earlier on the lower-layer file can keep referring to it, so reads through fd1 may not see writes made through fd2. Docker's overlay2 docs describe this open(2) caveat. Programs that hold files open across modifications are safer writing to volumes.

stem: An image based on a recent Ubuntu release starts fine on a modern host but crashes on a server running a very old kernel, with errors like `FATAL: kernel too old` or ENOSYS from new syscalls. Why can't the container fix this itself?

options.text: The image's embedded kernel is ignored in favour of the host's
options.why: Images contain no kernel at all, so there is nothing to ignore.

options.text: The image is only userspace; syscalls hit the old host kernel
options.why: New glibc or apps calling newer syscalls fail on an old kernel.

options.text: Docker filters syscalls the host can't emulate, through its seccomp profile
options.why: seccomp blocks syscalls deliberately; it doesn't emulate missing ones.

options.text: overlay2 can't mount layers that were built on a newer kernel
options.why: Layer formats don't depend on the build kernel's version.

explanation: A container carries libraries and binaries, but every system call goes to the host kernel. Userspace that expects newer kernel features (glibc checks the minimum version at start, or a program uses a newer syscall such as `clone3`) fails on an old kernel. Container portability is "same kernel ABI or newer", which is why base images document minimum host kernels.
reference: Docker docs: What is a container?; glibc release notes

stem: A container runs as root (UID 0) with Docker's default settings and no user-namespace remapping. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Its root is UID 0 on the host, so files it writes to a bind mount are owned by host root
options.why: Without a user namespace, UIDs inside and outside are identical.

options.text: It runs with a reduced capability set that, for example, excludes CAP_SYS_ADMIN
options.why: Docker drops many capabilities by default, so container root is weaker than host root.

options.text: It is mapped to the unprivileged `nobody` user on the host
options.why: That only happens with user namespaces, which aren't on by default.

options.text: It can load kernel modules, because modules apply only to its namespace
options.why: Modules are global; CAP_SYS_MODULE is dropped and seccomp blocks the syscalls.

options.text: It can mount any filesystem, because it owns its mount namespace
options.why: Mounting needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which the default capability set doesn't include.

explanation: By default container root is the real UID 0, so a breakout or a writable bind mount acts with host root's identity. What limits it is the reduced capability set (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE and so on), the default seccomp profile and AppArmor or SELinux. Hence the advice to run as a non-root USER and consider rootless mode or userns-remap.
reference: Docker docs: Docker security (Linux kernel capabilities)

stem: On a Docker host you run `ctr containers list` (containerd's CLI) and see no containers, although `docker ps` shows ten running. Why?

options.text: Docker uses its own built-in runtime, not containerd, in recent versions
options.why: Docker Engine still runs containers through containerd.

options.text: Docker uses containerd namespace `moby`; ctr shows `default`
options.why: containerd namespaces separate clients; use `ctr -n moby containers list`.

options.text: `ctr` hides running containers without `--running`
options.why: ctr lists containers regardless of state; the namespace is the issue.

options.text: The containers belong to the docker group, and ctr needs sudo to see them
options.why: Permission problems would cause an error, not an empty list.

explanation: containerd supports namespaces so multiple clients can share one daemon without seeing each other's objects. Docker Engine keeps its containers in the `moby` namespace, Kubernetes (through CRI) uses `k8s.io`, and `ctr` defaults to `default`. Pass `-n moby` to see Docker's containers, and don't manage them with ctr behind dockerd's back.

stem: The daemon uses `userns-remap`. A container bind-mounts `/srv/data`, whose files are owned by host UID 1000, which falls outside the container's mapped UID range. Inside the container, `ls -l` shows those files owned by which user?

options.text: UID 1000, unchanged, because bind mounts bypass user namespaces
options.why: Bind mounts are seen through the container's user namespace mapping.

options.text: root, because the remapped root owns everything it can see
options.why: Ownership is translated per ID, and root inside maps to one specific host UID.

options.text: The overflow user, UID 65534 (`nobody`)
options.why: Host IDs with no mapping inside the namespace appear as the overflow UID.

options.text: UID 101000, offset by the subordinate range start
options.why: The offset applies to mapped IDs; 1000 isn't in the mapped range.

explanation: In a user namespace, file owners are translated through the UID map. A host UID that has no mapping inside the namespace shows as the overflow UID, usually 65534 (`nobody`), and the container's root usually can't write to such files. Shared data directories must be owned by remapped IDs when userns-remap is on.

stem: On a cgroup v2 host with a current Docker Engine and default settings, what does `cat /proc/self/cgroup` print inside a container?

options.text: `0::/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope`, the full host cgroup path
options.why: That path would appear with `--cgroupns=host`, not with the default.

options.text: `0::/`, because the container has a private cgroup namespace
options.why: Docker defaults to a private cgroup namespace on cgroup v2, so its cgroup looks like the root.

options.text: One line per controller, such as `4:memory:/docker/<id>`
options.why: Per-controller lines are cgroup v1 format; v2 has one unified hierarchy.

options.text: Nothing, because /proc/self/cgroup is hidden from containers
options.why: The file exists and is readable in containers.

explanation: With cgroup v2 Docker creates a private cgroup namespace by default, so the container's cgroup appears as the root of its view and `/proc/self/cgroup` shows `0::/`. That hides the host's cgroup layout and lets tools inside treat `/sys/fs/cgroup` as their own limits. `--cgroupns=host` would expose the full host path instead.

stem: A binary compiled on Ubuntu is copied into an `alpine` image. The file exists and is executable, yet running it prints `sh: ./app: not found`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Alpine mounts /app with noexec, so the shell can't see the file
options.why: noexec would give "Permission denied", not "not found".

options.text: Its glibc loader (`ld-linux`) doesn't exist on musl-based Alpine
options.why: The kernel can't find the requested dynamic loader, which surfaces as "not found".

options.text: The binary targets a newer kernel than the Alpine image ships with
options.why: Images don't ship kernels; it would run on the host kernel.

options.text: Alpine's shell can only start binaries that were installed through apk
options.why: apk installation isn't required for executables.

explanation: A dynamically linked glibc binary names its loader, such as `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, in its ELF header. Alpine uses musl and has no such file, so `execve` fails with ENOENT and the shell reports "not found" even though the binary is present. Build on Alpine, link statically, or use a glibc-based image such as Debian slim.
